title: Book I: Miss Brooke — Chapter V
paragraphs:
“Hard students are commonly troubled with gowts, catarrhs, rheums,
cachexia, bradypepsia, bad eyes, stone, and collick, crudities,
oppilations, vertigo, winds, consumptions, and all such diseases as
come by over-much sitting: they are most part lean, dry, ill-colored …
and all through immoderate pains and extraordinary studies. If you will
not believe the truth of this, look upon great Tostatus and Thomas
Aquinas’ works; and tell me whether those men took pains.”—BURTON’S
_Anatomy of Melancholy_, P. I, s. 2.
Here is the letter Mr. Casaubon wrote.

MY DEAR MISS BROOKE,—Your guardian has permitted me to write to you on a matter closer to my heart than any other. I trust I am right in seeing more than a coincidence of dates in the fact that I became aware of a need in my own life just when the possibility of knowing you arose. Within the first hour of our meeting, I felt you were eminently, perhaps uniquely, fitted to meet that need. I may say that this need involved stirrings of affection which even my absorption in a work too specialized to abandon could not continually conceal. Every subsequent opportunity to observe you has deepened that impression, convincing me still more strongly of the suitability I first perceived, and so calling forth more decisively the affections I have just mentioned. Our conversations have, I think, sufficiently explained the character of my life and purposes—a character I know is unsuited to the more ordinary kind of mind. In you, however, I have recognized an elevation of thought and a capacity for devotion which I had never supposed could accompany either youth’s early bloom or those feminine graces that both win distinction and bestow it when joined, as they notably are in you, to the intellectual qualities already described. I confess I had not hoped to find this rare union of the substantial and the attractive, suited both to assist with serious labours and to lend charm to unoccupied hours. Had I not been introduced to you—an event which, let me repeat, I trust is not merely coincidental with those emerging needs, but providentially connected to them as stages in completing a life’s plan—I would presumably have continued to the end without trying to relieve my solitude through marriage. Such, my dear Miss Brooke, is an accurate account of my feelings. Relying on your kindly indulgence, I now venture to ask how far your own feelings might confirm my happy anticipation. I would regard your accepting me as your husband and the earthly guardian of your welfare as the highest gift of Providence. In return I can at least offer an affection not previously spent, and the faithful dedication of a life which, however little of it remains, contains no past pages where, should you turn them, you would discover records that could rightly give you either bitterness or shame. I await your feelings with an anxiety that wisdom would advise me, if possible, to divert through harder work than usual. But in this kind of experience I am still young. When I consider an unfavourable outcome, I cannot help feeling that resignation to solitude will be harder after hope has briefly lit it.

Whatever your answer, I shall remain,
Yours in sincere devotion,
EDWARD CASAUBON.

Dorothea trembled as she read, then dropped to her knees, covered her face and sobbed. She could not pray. In the flood of solemn feeling, thoughts blurred and images drifted uncertainly; she could only cast herself, with a child’s sense of resting, into the lap of a divine consciousness that sustained her own. She stayed like that until it was time to dress for dinner.

How could she have thought of examining the letter critically as a declaration of love? The fact that a fuller life was opening before her possessed her whole soul. She was a novice about to enter a higher degree of initiation. Now there would be room for the energies that stirred restlessly beneath the obscurity and weight of her ignorance and the petty tyranny of the world’s habits.

Now she could devote herself to duties both great and definite; now she could live constantly in the light of a mind she revered. This hope also glowed with proud delight: a girl’s joyful surprise at being chosen by the man her admiration had chosen. All Dorothea’s passion passed through a mind striving towards an ideal life. The radiance of her transformed girlhood fell on the first object within its reach. The day’s small events, which had stirred her dissatisfaction with her actual circumstances, added force to the speed with which inclination became resolve.

After dinner, while Celia played an “air, with variations”—a little tinkling representative of the artistic part of the girls’ education—Dorothea went upstairs to answer Mr. Casaubon. Why delay? She wrote the letter three times, not to alter its words but because her hand was unusually unsteady. She could not bear to have him think her handwriting poor or illegible. She prided herself on a hand in which each letter could be identified without extensive guesswork, and intended to make much use of this skill to spare his eyes. Three times she wrote.

MY DEAR MR. CASAUBON,—I am deeply grateful that you love me and consider me worthy to become your wife. I can imagine no greater happiness than one inseparable from yours. To say more would only repeat the same thing at greater length, for I can think of nothing now except the hope that throughout life I may remain

Devotedly yours,
DOROTHEA BROOKE.

Later that evening she followed her uncle into the library and gave him the letter to send in the morning. He was surprised, but showed it only by a few moments of silence. He moved various things about on his desk, then stood with his back to the fire and his glasses on his nose, looking at the address on Dorothea’s letter.
“Have you given this enough thought, my dear?” he finally asked.
“I didn’t need to think for long, uncle. I know of no reason to hesitate. Anything that changed my mind would have to be important and entirely new to me.”
“Ah! So you’ve accepted him? Then Chettam has no chance? Has he offended you—offended you, you know? What don’t you like about Chettam?”
“There’s nothing about him that I do like,” Dorothea answered rather hastily.
Mr. Brooke jerked his head and shoulders back as if somebody had tossed a small object at him. Dorothea immediately reproached herself and added—
“I mean as a husband. I think he’s very kind—really very good about the cottages. A man with good intentions.”

“But you must have a scholar and all that? Well, it does run in our family a little. I had it myself—that love of knowledge, looking into everything. A little too much; it carried me too far. It doesn’t often run down the female line, though. Or it goes underground like those rivers in Greece, you know, then comes out in the sons. Clever sons, clever mothers. I studied that quite a bit once. Still, my dear, I’ve always said people should do as they choose in these matters, up to a point. As your guardian I couldn’t have agreed to a bad match. But Casaubon has good standing, a good position. I’m afraid Chettam will be hurt, though, and Mrs. Cadwallader will blame me.”

Of course Celia knew nothing of these events that evening. She put Dorothea’s distracted manner, and the signs of more tears since they came home, down to her anger about Sir James Chettam and the cottages. She took care not to cause further offence. Once she had said her piece, Celia had no wish to revisit unpleasant subjects. Even as a child she never quarrelled with anyone; she simply observed with surprise that they quarrelled with her and looked like turkey-cocks, then was ready to play cat’s cradle as soon as they recovered. Dorothea had always found something wrong in her sister’s remarks, though Celia privately protested that she only ever said how things were, nothing more. She never did, and never could, invent things to say out of her own head. But Dodo’s great virtue was that she did not stay angry for long. Now, despite their scarcely having spoken all evening, when Celia put her work away to go to bed—as she always did much earlier—Dorothea spoke from the low stool where she had sat, unable to do anything but think. In moments of deep, quiet feeling, her musical voice made her words sound like a beautiful passage of recitative—
“Celia, dear, come here and kiss me,” she said, opening her arms.
Celia knelt to reach the right height and gave her a little butterfly kiss. Dorothea gently wrapped her arms around her and solemnly kissed first one cheek, then the other.
“Don’t stay up, Dodo. You’re so pale tonight. Go to bed soon,” Celia said comfortably, without a hint of pathos.
“No, dear, I’m very, very happy,” Dorothea answered with fervour.
“All the better,” Celia thought. “But how strangely Dodo swings from one extreme to another.”
At lunch the next day, the butler handed Mr. Brooke something and said, “Jonas is back, sir. He brought this letter.”
Mr. Brooke read it, then nodded towards Dorothea. “Casaubon, my dear. He’s coming to dinner. He didn’t wait to write more—didn’t wait, you know.”

There was nothing unusual in a dinner guest being announced to her sister in advance. But following her uncle’s glance, Celia was struck by the peculiar effect on Dorothea. Something like a reflected white wing in sunlight seemed to sweep across her face, ending in one of her rare blushes. For the first time Celia wondered whether there might be more between Mr. Casaubon and her sister than his pleasure in learned conversation and hers in listening. Until now she had put Dorothea’s admiration for this “ugly,” scholarly acquaintance in the same category as her admiration for Monsieur Liret at Lausanne, also ugly and learned. Dorothea had never tired of listening to old Monsieur Liret even when Celia’s feet were freezing and the sight of the skin moving over his bald head had become positively dreadful. Why shouldn’t her enthusiasm for Mr. Casaubon be of exactly the same kind? Besides, all learned men probably viewed young people rather as schoolmasters did.

Now, however, the suspicion flashing into Celia’s mind truly startled her. Such surprises were rare: her extraordinary quickness at noticing certain kinds of signs usually prepared her for the outward events that interested her. She did not yet imagine Mr. Casaubon an accepted suitor. She had merely begun to feel disgust at the possibility of anything in Dorothea’s mind tending that way. Here was something genuinely upsetting about Dodo. Refusing Sir James Chettam was all very well, but marrying Mr. Casaubon! Celia felt a kind of shame mixed with a sense of absurdity. Yet perhaps Dodo, if she really approached such extravagance, could be turned aside. Experience had often shown that one could count on her susceptibility to impressions. The day was damp, so they would not go walking. They went upstairs to their sitting room, where Celia noticed that instead of settling industriously to some occupation, Dorothea simply propped her elbow on an open book and gazed out at the great cedar, silvered by moisture. Celia herself began making a toy for the curate’s children. She had no intention of rushing into any subject.

Dorothea was indeed thinking Celia ought to know how momentously Mr. Casaubon’s position had changed since his last visit. It hardly seemed fair to leave her ignorant of something that must affect her manner towards him, yet she could not help shrinking from telling her. Dorothea blamed herself for a certain pettiness in this fear. She hated having small anxieties or schemes about her actions, but just now she was seeking the highest possible help against her dread of Celia’s pretty, worldly-minded prose and its corrosive power. Her reverie broke, and the difficulty of deciding vanished, when Celia’s small, rather throaty voice spoke in its usual tone of an aside, or a “by the way.”
“Is anyone coming to dinner apart from Mr. Casaubon?”
“Nobody that I’ve heard of.”
“I hope someone else is. Then I won’t have to listen to him eating his soup like that.”
“What’s so remarkable about the way he eats soup?”
“Really, Dodo, don’t you hear him scraping his spoon? And he always blinks before he speaks. I don’t know whether Locke blinked, but if he did, I’m certainly sorry for anyone sitting opposite him.”
“Celia,” Dorothea said with emphatic seriousness, “please don’t make any more remarks like that.”
“Why shouldn’t I? They’re perfectly true,” Celia replied. She had reasons to persist, although she was beginning to feel afraid.
“Plenty of things are true that only the most commonplace minds notice.”

“Then commonplace minds must be rather useful. I think it’s a pity Mr. Casaubon’s mother wasn’t more commonplace. She might have taught him better manners.” Having thrown this little spear, Celia felt frightened inside and ready to flee.
Dorothea’s feelings had built into an avalanche; there was no possibility of further preparation.
“I ought to tell you, Celia, that Mr. Casaubon and I are engaged to be married.”

Perhaps Celia had never been so pale. Only her habitual care for anything in her hands saved the paper man she was making from an injured leg. She immediately set the fragile figure down and sat absolutely still for a few moments. A tear was forming when she spoke.
“Oh, Dodo, I hope you’ll be happy.” At this moment her sisterly tenderness necessarily overcame her other feelings, and her fears arose from love.
Dorothea remained distressed and deeply hurt.
“So it’s all settled?” Celia asked in a hushed, awed voice. “And does uncle know?”
“I’ve accepted Mr. Casaubon’s proposal. Uncle brought me his letter, and he already knew what it contained.”

“Forgive me if I’ve said anything hurtful, Dodo,” Celia said with a small sob. She could never have imagined feeling as she did. The whole business had something of a funeral about it, with Mr. Casaubon as the officiating clergyman, whom it would be indecent to comment on.
“Never mind, Kitty. Don’t be upset. We could never admire the same people. I often offend in much the same way; I tend to speak too harshly of people I don’t like.”

Despite her generosity, Dorothea still smarted, perhaps as much at Celia’s quiet astonishment as at her little criticisms. Naturally everyone around Tipton would be unsympathetic to the marriage. She knew nobody who shared her view of life and its highest purposes.

Nevertheless, before the evening ended she was very happy. During an hour’s _tête-à-tête_ with Mr. Casaubon, she spoke more freely than ever, pouring out her joy at the prospect of devoting herself to him and learning how best to share and further his great aims. This childlike, unrestrained ardour moved him to an unfamiliar delight—what man would have been unmoved? He was not surprised to be its object—what lover would have been?

“My dear young lady—Miss Brooke—Dorothea!” he said, enclosing her hand in both of his. “This happiness exceeds anything I ever imagined might await me. I had never conceived of meeting someone whose mind and person united so richly the graces that could make marriage desirable. You possess all—more than all—the qualities I have always considered the distinctive virtues of womanhood. Your sex’s greatest charm is its capacity for passionate, self-sacrificing affection; in this we recognize its fitness to round out and complete the existence of our own. Until now my pleasures have mostly been of the more austere kind: the satisfactions of a solitary scholar. I have had little inclination to gather flowers that would fade in my hand, but now I shall eagerly pick them to lay upon your breast.”

No speech could have been more honest in intention. Its chilly closing rhetoric was as sincere as a dog’s bark or a courting rook’s caw. Wouldn’t it be rash to suppose there was no passion behind those sonnets to Delia that sound to us like a mandolin’s thin music?

Dorothea’s faith supplied everything his words left unstated. What believer finds a troubling omission or clumsy phrase? A prophet’s or poet’s text stretches to contain whatever we can put into it; even its bad grammar becomes sublime.

“I’m very ignorant. You’ll be astonished at how little I know,” Dorothea said. “I have so many thoughts that may be entirely mistaken, and now I’ll be able to tell you them all and ask you about them. But,” she added, quickly imagining how he might feel, “I won’t trouble you too much—only when you want to listen. You must often be tired from pursuing your own subjects. It will be gain enough for me if you’ll let me accompany you there.”

“How could I now continue along any path without your company?” Mr. Casaubon said, kissing her candid forehead and feeling heaven had bestowed a blessing exactly suited to his particular needs. Without knowing it, he was being influenced by the charm of a nature entirely free of hidden calculations, whether for immediate effect or distant purposes. That was what made Dorothea so childlike and, in some people’s opinion, so foolish despite her reputed cleverness. Here, for example, she was figuratively throwing herself at Mr. Casaubon’s feet and kissing his unfashionable shoe ties as if he were a Protestant Pope. She was doing nothing to teach him to wonder whether he deserved her; she merely asked herself anxiously how she could deserve him. Before he left the next day, they had agreed to marry within six weeks. Why wait? His house stood ready. It was no parsonage but a substantial mansion with extensive land. The curate lived in the parsonage and carried out every duty except preaching the morning sermon.
